t: Find The First Player to win K Games in a Row
o: Players fight in queue order; the winner stays at the front, the loser goes to the back. We simulate until someone wins k straight games. Since skills are unique, once the current front player is the global maximum they win forever, so the simulation terminates quickly — at most n games before the maximum reaches the front, after which it accumulates wins indefinitely. Hence a simple O(n) pointer simulation suffices despite k up to 1e9.
k: Never use a real queue — just track the current champion's skill and index plus a win streak.
Once the champion's skill exceeds all remaining unplayed opponents, they will win k in a row; if the loop ends first, the champion (the global max) is the answer.

a.n: Approach 1: Linear simulation with a champion pointer
a.i: Keep the reigning champion; compare against each subsequent player once. Wins increment the streak; a loss transfers championship and resets the streak to 1.
s: For each next player: if champion's skill is higher, streak++; otherwise the challenger becomes champion with streak = 1.
If streak reaches k, return the champion's index.
If the loop finishes, the champion is the global maximum and will win indefinitely — return its index.
a.t: O(n) — each player challenges the champion exactly once before the max takes over permanently
a.sp: O(1) — only pointers and a counter

a.i: Literally maintain a deque of player indices, popping two, pushing the loser to the back, and keeping the winner at the front. Early-exit when the front player's skill equals the global maximum and the streak keeps growing.
s: Initialize a deque with indices 0..n-1 and streak = 0.
Pop the front two players; the higher-skill one wins.
Winner goes back to the front, loser to the back; update the streak.
Stop when streak == k; this is worst-case O(n·something) but terminates fast because the max sweeps the queue in one pass.
a.t: O(n) amortized — the maximum clears the queue once, then wins forever; the loop exits within O(n) steps after that point because the streak grows monotonically once the max is champion

w: Always prefer Approach 1: it is shorter, uses O(1) space, and cannot TLE. The classic mistake is simulating k up to 1e9 games naively — recognize that the global maximum ends the game logically. Edge cases: k = 1 (answer is whoever wins the first game), and n = 2. Follow-up: what if skills could tie, or if losers re-enter with reduced skill?
